title: Sex, Gender, and Social Construction
description: Where the sex and gender distinction came from, and why it is argued over today

concepts.title: Two Words for Two Things
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do girls and boys so often end up in different school subjects, jobs and household chores? One answer is biology; another is society. To pull the two apart, sociologists use two words. Sex names biological traits such as chromosomes, hormones and reproductive anatomy. Gender names the meanings, expectations and roles a society attaches to being a woman or a man: how you are expected to dress, speak, work, care and compete.

The split came from medicine before it reached sociology. To explain why some people felt trapped in the wrong bodies, Robert Stoller began in 1968 to use sex for biological traits and gender for the amount of femininity and masculinity a person showed.1 Feminists quickly saw its political use. If many differences between women and men were socially produced, they were also changeable.

In Britain the distinction entered sociology through a 1972 book by Ann Oakley, written when she was 27:2 Sex, Gender and Society. Oakley gathered biological, psychological, medical and anthropological research to argue that culture, more than biology, shapes many of the differences people treat as natural. She drew on cross-cultural work such as Margaret Mead's Sex and Temperament (1935), which described societies that defined masculinity and femininity very differently, although Mead's observations were later disputed by the anthropologist Derek Freeman.

The distinction changed how research is done. If gender is social, it can vary by place and period, so you can study it the way you study class or religion: compare societies, trace change over time and ask who gains. Simone de Beauvoir had made the philosophical case in 1949 with her claim that one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman, which the existentialism topic explores. Oakley turned the idea into a research programme. The rest of this lesson asks how firmly the line between sex and gender holds.

concepts.title: Learned or Given? The John/Joan Case
concepts.contentHtml:
If gender is social, how does it get inside us? The classic answer is socialisation: children learn what their culture expects of girls and boys from parents, peers, schools and media, and come to want what they are expected to want. The writer Kate Millett put it strongly in 1971, describing gender differences as having essentially cultural, rather than biological, bases that result from differential treatment.

The most famous test of the idea went badly wrong. Bruce Reimer was born in Winnipeg in 1965, one of identical twin boys. A failed circumcision irreparably damaged his penis in infancy, and on the advice of the psychologist John Money his parents raised him as a girl, with surgery and female hormones. Money described the transition as successful and contrasted the child's girlish behaviour with the twin brother's boyishness.1 Reporting it as the anonymous John/Joan case, he used it to justify sex reassignment surgery for children with intersex conditions or damaged genitals.

In 1997 the psychologist Milton Diamond and Keith Sigmundson published a long-term follow-up. The child had rejected the sex of rearing and switched at puberty to living as a male, later known as David Reimer. They urged doctors to rethink the standard advice to raise infant boys with severe penile injuries as girls. Reimer spoke publicly about the trauma of his treatment, and he died by suicide in 2004, aged 38.

What does the case show? Many read it as strong evidence that gender identity has biological roots that upbringing cannot simply overwrite. Others caution that one traumatic case cannot settle a nature versus nurture question, since so much else in this child's life was unusual. Most sociologists now accept that biology and social life both shape gender, and study how they interact rather than asking which one wins.

concepts.title: Is Sex Itself Social?
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1990s the neat split between biological sex and social gender was under attack from two opposite directions, and the argument is still live.

The first challenge says sex is less tidy than the split assumes. Reviewing the medical literature, Anne Fausto-Sterling estimated in 2000 that about 1.7% of people do not fall neatly within the usual sex classifications. Leonard Sax replied in 2002 that this figure counted conditions most clinicians do not call intersex, such as Klinefelter syndrome, Turner syndrome and late-onset adrenal hyperplasia. Restricting the term to cases where chromosomal sex is inconsistent with anatomy, or where anatomy cannot be classed as male or female, he put the rate at about 0.018%, almost 100 times lower.1 The numbers differ mainly because the definitions differ.

The second challenge goes further. Judith Butler argued in Gender Trouble (1990) that distinguishing biological sex from social gender is unintelligible, because sex is as socially constructed as gender. Butler does not deny that physical bodies exist.2 The claim is that we only ever understand bodies through social categories, so the belief that humans naturally come in two sexes is itself a product of gendered practice. Lesson 2 returns to Butler.

From the other side, gender-critical feminists and philosophers argue that sex is real, binary in all but a tiny fraction of cases, and politically important. The philosopher Alex Byrne holds that women are simply adult human females, and Holly Lawford-Smith treats woman and man as sex terms, with femininity and masculinity as the social norms laid on top. On this view, folding sex into gender hides sex-based facts that law, medicine and statistics need, a point Lesson 7 takes up.

Notice what kind of disagreement this is. Part of it is empirical: how often do sex characteristics diverge? Much of it is about which categories our words, laws and statistics should track. Keep those two questions apart and the debate becomes far easier to follow.

title: Doing Gender, Performativity, and Queer Theory
description: Gender as something you do: interaction, performativity and the queer critique

concepts.title: Doing Gender
concepts.contentHtml:
Watch a toddler being told that big boys don't cry, or an adult lowering their voice for a job interview, and you are watching gender being made. In a 1987 article in the journal Gender & Society, the sociologists Candace West and Don Zimmerman proposed that gender is not a trait you have but something you do. They described it as a routine, methodical and recurring accomplishment, produced in everyday interaction.1 Their approach comes from ethnomethodology, the study of how people produce a sense of social order, which the modern social theory topic introduces alongside Goffman.

They separated three things:

  • Sex: a classification made by applying socially agreed biological criteria, such as genitals at birth or chromosomes before birth.
  • Sex category: the classification others make of you at a glance, from displays such as clothing, hair and voice. Nobody checks chromosomes at a bus stop.
  • Gender: managing your conduct in light of what is thought appropriate for your sex category.

Their key case came from Harold Garfinkel's 1967 study of Agnes, who was raised as a boy, adopted a female identity at age 17 and had sex reassignment surgery several years later. Agnes developed a set of deliberate procedures for passing as a "normal, natural female", both before and after surgery. What most people do without noticing, she had to do on purpose, and that made the hidden work of gender visible.

The central idea is accountability. People know their actions can be described, judged and explained by others, and they shape them with an eye to how they will look. West and Zimmerman drew a sobering conclusion: when we do gender appropriately, we sustain, reproduce and legitimate the institutions built on sex category. When we fail, it is we as individuals, not the institutions, who are called to account. Gender can in principle be done differently, but the costs of doing it differently fall on the person.

concepts.title: Butler and Performativity
concepts.contentHtml:
Judith Butler's Gender Trouble (1990), which the literary criticism topic touches on, pushed constructionism to its limit. Most feminist accounts, Butler argued, assume a gender core: some inner womanhood or manhood from which feminine or masculine behaviour flows. Butler denies that any such core exists. Gender is not a stable identity from which acts follow; it is instituted through a stylised repetition of habitual acts, from ways of walking and dressing to ways of speaking and desiring, repeated until they seem natural.1

That is what performative means here: the acts produce the very identity they appear to express. If nobody performed gendered acts, there would be no genders at all. Hence Butler's political aims: to loosen the norms that compel people to act in gendering ways, and to treat woman as an open-ended term, a becoming rather than a fixed thing.

A common misreading is that Butler thinks you pick your gender each morning like an outfit. The argument is closer to the opposite. The acts are compelled by norms you learned long before you could choose, and repeated under social pressure; that repetition is why gender feels like nature. Performativity is not free performance.

Butler's influence across the humanities is enormous, and so is the criticism. In a 1999 essay titled "The Professor of Parody", the philosopher Martha Nussbaum attacked Butler's dense prose and argued that the theory reduces feminism to symbolic verbal politics: finding small spaces within power to parody and transgress, instead of changing laws and institutions that shape real women's lives. She called the result a dangerous quietism.2 Defenders answer that the critique of fixed categories opened room for new ones; the philosopher Robin Dembroff, for example, treats genderqueer as a real gender kind that unsettles the binary. Gender-critical feminists, met in Lesson 1, reject the starting claim that sex is social at all.

concepts.title: Queer Theory and the History of Sexuality
concepts.contentHtml:
If gender is made, what about sexuality? Queer theory, which took shape in the late 1980s and early 1990s around the work of Butler and Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, turns the same suspicion on sexual categories. Sedgwick argued in 1990 that much of modern Western thought silently relies on a very recent and arbitrary split of the sexual world into two species, heterosexual and homosexual.

History gives the claim its force. The ancient Greeks had no terms that match our heterosexual and homosexual pair; their distinctions turned on age, social status and role in the sex act. From the 1970s, researchers influenced by Mary McIntosh and Michel Foucault (whose theory of power belongs to the modern theory topic) argued that sexual categories, and the identities attached to them, are made by history. On this view homosexuality as a kind of person is a solely modern, Western concept and role.1 This position is social constructionism. Its rival, essentialism, holds that same-sex attraction is a universal human pattern that cultures merely name differently. Before queer theory, the poet Adrienne Rich had linked the dominance of heterosexuality to patriarchy in her 1980 essay on compulsory heterosexuality.

Can measurement settle the argument? Not alone, but it narrows the options. In 2019 a genome-wide study of 477,522 people found five genetic loci linked to same-sex sexual behaviour.2 All the tested variants together accounted for 8 to 25% of the variation in that behaviour, overlapped only partly between men and women, and could not meaningfully predict any individual's behaviour. The study also found no single continuum running from opposite-sex to same-sex behaviour.

Each side can claim something here. Biology matters, but not as a single gene that fixes orientation; and the tidy categories we use may not match how desire is actually distributed across people.

title: Feminisms and Intersectionality
description: Feminist strands, Crenshaw's intersectionality, and how to test and criticise it

concepts.title: Waves and Strands of Feminism
concepts.contentHtml:
The politics topic tells the story of feminism in waves. The first wave in the English-speaking world, from the 1840s to the 1920s, won the vote and a language of equal rights, though its campaigns were aimed mainly at middle-class white women.1 The second wave, from the 1960s, borrowed the language of liberation from the civil rights movements. Many historians find the wave image too tidy, but it marks a real shift from formal rights to the politics of everyday life.

That shift mattered for sociology. The slogan "the personal is political" claimed that housework, sex, marriage and harassment were not private troubles but parts of a social structure. In consciousness-raising groups women compared experiences each had thought were hers alone, and out of that comparison came new concepts such as sexual harassment and objectification. Turning shared experience into named concepts is close to what sociologists do with data.

Feminists also disagreed about causes and cures. Alison Jaggar's 1983 survey grouped feminist political theory into four camps: liberal, socialist, Marxist and radical feminism. In brief:

  • Liberal feminism: remove legal and customary barriers so that women can compete as equals.
  • Radical feminism: male dominance is the root structure, reaching into sexuality itself. Catharine MacKinnon put it starkly in 1987: "Power/powerlessness is the sex difference".
  • Marxist and socialist feminism: capitalism profits from the sexual division of labour and from women's unpaid work at home; some, such as Mariarosa Dalla Costa (1974) and Silvia Federici (1975), demanded wages for housework.

These strands predict different findings. A liberal expects gaps to shrink as barriers fall; a radical expects inequality to reappear in new forms; a socialist feminist looks first at unpaid care. Lessons 5 and 6 test those expectations against the data.

concepts.title: Crenshaw and the Intersection
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1976, five Black women who worked on the assembly line at General Motors in St Louis sued the company.1 Its seniority system laid off the last hired first, and they argued it discriminated against them as Black women. In DeGraffenreid v. General Motors the court rejected them. It ruled that the law let them claim race discrimination or sex discrimination, but not a combination of both.2 Because GM had kept on some women, all of them white, and some Black workers, all of them men, neither claim succeeded.

In 1989 the legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw used this case to coin intersectionality. Her image was a crossroads: when an accident happens where traffic arrives from several directions, the harm cannot always be blamed on one road. The fault in anti-discrimination law, she argued, was its single-axis framework, which treats race and sex as mutually exclusive categories. That framework quietly takes the most privileged members of each group as the model, such as Black men in race cases and white women in sex cases, and Black women fall into the gap between them.

The idea is older than the name. Historians trace it back to Sojourner Truth's 1851 speech "Ar'n't I a Woman?", and in 1977 the Combahee River Collective of Black feminists wrote of interlocking systems of oppression. Patricia Hill Collins later used that phrase for the large-scale structures of race, class and gender, keeping intersectionality for how individuals are positioned within them.

Crenshaw herself has resisted the term's inflation. In a Columbia Law School interview she called intersectionality a lens for seeing where power comes and collides, and said that some people look to it as a grand theory of everything, but that this is not her intention.

concepts.title: Testing and Criticising Intersectionality
concepts.contentHtml:
Intersectionality spread fast. In 2005 the sociologist Leslie McCall called it the most important contribution that women's studies, with other fields, had made so far. A popular idea still has to earn its keep as a research tool, though, and here there are real disputes.

Start with measurement. Suppose you study pay. An additive model says a Black woman's disadvantage equals the gap for being Black plus the gap for being a woman. An intersectional, non-additive model says the combination can differ from that sum: larger, smaller, or different in kind. In statistics this is an interaction effect, and it can be tested by comparing the observed combined gap with the additive prediction. In 2016 the philosophers Liam Kofi Bright, Daniel Malinsky and Morgan Thompson noted that social scientists report difficulties in drawing out testable predictions from intersectionality theory, and showed how causal modelling can turn core claims such as non-additivity into hypotheses that data can support or refute. Other scholars reply that some intersectional claims concern qualitatively different experiences that no regression term captures.

The theoretical criticisms come mostly from sympathisers:

  • Missing structure. Collins argued that intersectionality describes individual positions well but needs a macro-level account of the interlocking systems that create those positions.
  • Who counts? Jennifer Nash asked whether all identities are intersectional or only those of people marginalised in several ways at once.1 If only the latter, the theory may miss how privilege works.

In public debate the term has become a political flashpoint, which the politics and postmodernism topics trace. A fair summary: as a claim that disadvantages can combine in non-additive ways, intersectionality is testable, and researchers test it. As a grand theory of identity it is contested, and Crenshaw herself does not offer it as one.

title: Masculinities
description: Connell's hegemonic masculinity, its critics, and the gaps where men fall behind

concepts.title: Hegemonic Masculinity
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades gender research mostly meant research on women. The study of masculinities, plural on purpose, changed that, and its central concept came from an unlikely place: a field study of social inequality in Australian high schools, reported by Kessler and colleagues in 1982.1 The sociologist R. W. Connell developed it, alongside work on men's bodies and on men in Australian labour politics, into the idea of hegemonic masculinity.

The word hegemony comes from Gramsci's Marxist writing on how class relations are stabilised, here transferred to gender. Hegemonic masculinity is the currently most honoured way of being a man in a given setting. It requires other men to position themselves in relation to it, and it legitimates men's dominance over women. Two features are easy to miss:

  • It is normative, not statistical. Only a minority of men may actually enact it, as with the ideal of the tough, unflinching breadwinner that few men match.2
  • It works mainly through consent. Hegemony means ascendancy through culture, institutions and persuasion; it can be backed by force, but it is not the same as violence.

Around the hegemonic form sit others. Subordinated masculinities are pushed below it; early work on the concept drew on research into gay men's ambivalent relationship to conventional masculinity. Complicit masculinity describes the many men who receive the benefits of patriarchy without enacting a strong version of masculine dominance.

The concept explains a puzzle. Many individual men do not feel powerful, yet men as a group hold most positions of power. Hegemonic masculinity lets you see both at once: dominance can be organised around an ideal that most men never fully match.

concepts.title: Critics, Revisions and "Toxic" Masculinity
concepts.contentHtml:
The concept spread rapidly. By 2005 more than 200 papers used the exact phrase hegemonic masculinity in their titles or abstracts, in fields from education and anti-violence work to health and counselling. That year Connell and James Messerschmidt reviewed five principal criticisms that had built up since the early 1990s.1

The sharpest was reification: the charge that the concept hardens into a fixed character type, a list of bad traits, and in practice reduces to power or toxicity. Connell and Messerschmidt conceded that the criticism of trait models and rigid typologies is sound. They agreed that in some settings hegemonic masculinity does involve violence, but insisted that hegemony has numerous configurations, defined by what sustains dominance in a particular setting, not by a checklist.

The revision kept the core: masculinities are plural, and they are arranged in a hierarchy. It dropped the trait lists, gave more weight to women's agency, distinguished local, regional and global levels, and paid more attention to change.

Outside academia the argument grew louder. In August 2018 the American Psychological Association's council voted on guidelines for psychological practice with boys and men, which presented some traditional masculinity norms, such as stoicism, as stopping men from seeking help. The psychologist Christopher Ferguson, a council member, warned that the guidelines lack a broad scientific base, particularly an understanding of biological contributors to gender identity, and that they used traditional masculinity as a stereotype. Supporters pointed to a long line of research linking rigid masculine norms to risky health behaviour, met in the next concept. The dispute is the reification problem in public: is a concept of masculinity describing patterns, or condemning men?

concepts.title: Boys and Men: Measured Gaps, Disputed Causes
concepts.contentHtml:
Some of the largest gender gaps in rich countries now run the other way. In the United States in 1970, 20% of men aged 25 to 34 held a bachelor's degree against 12% of women; by 2020 the figures were 32% for men and 41% for women.1 In England and Wales in 2024, the suicide rate was 17.6 deaths per 100,000 for males and 5.7 for females, roughly three to one.2 Across the UK, life expectancy at birth in 2022 to 2024 was 79.1 years for males and 83.0 for females.

Those are measurements. The interpretations differ, and each has serious defenders:

  • Masculinity norms. W. H. Courtenay argued in 2000 that health behaviours are one way of demonstrating masculinity: practices that undermine men's health, such as risk-taking, are often signifiers of masculinity that men use to negotiate power and status.
  • Biology. Zarulli and colleagues found in 2018 that women outlived men even in seven populations facing famine, epidemics and slavery. Newborn girls survived better than newborn boys, at ages when behavioural and social differences are minimal or favour boys, which supports a biological survival advantage that social factors then modulate.
  • Structural change. Richard Reeves, in Of Boys and Men (2022), stresses economic and social changes that have left many men losing ground in school, work and family, and argues that helping them is compatible with gender equality.

These explanations can all be partly true, and the hard question is how much each contributes in a given case. Note too that men's disadvantages and men's dominance are not contradictory in Connell's framework, which expects some men to pay heavy costs inside a system that advantages men as a group.

title: Measuring the Gender Pay Gap
description: What the pay gap measures, what explains it, and how discrimination is tested

concepts.title: One Number, Many Meanings
concepts.contentHtml:
Each autumn the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes the UK's gender pay gap from the Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings. It is the difference between men's and women's median hourly earnings, excluding overtime, as a percentage of men's. In April 2026 it was 6.8% for full-time employees, down from 7.2% in April 2025, 9.4% a decade earlier and 16.4% in 2001.1

Which gap you quote depends on whom you count. Among all employees the gap was 12.3% in April 2026. Among part-time employees it was negative 2.1%: women working part time earned slightly more per hour than men working part time. The all-employee gap is larger than either because many more women than men work part time, and part-time jobs pay less per hour. None of these numbers is wrong; each answers a different question.

Now the point most people miss. The ONS figure is a measure across all jobs, not a comparison of men and women doing the same job.2 Paying a woman less for equal work is a separate question, governed by equal pay law; the headline gap mostly reflects who does which jobs, for how many hours, and at what stage of life.

Age shows the pattern. In April 2026 the full-time gap was 0.3% for employees aged 18 to 21, 4.1% for those aged 30 to 39 and 8.2% for those aged 40 to 49, a jump the ONS says is largely explained by the impact of motherhood. Internationally, the gap in median full-time earnings across OECD countries in 2024 (or the latest year) averaged 10.1%, ranging from 29.0% in Korea to negative 8.4% in Luxembourg.3 That OECD measure uses full-time, full-year earnings rather than hourly pay, so it is not directly comparable with the ONS figure: a reminder to check the definition before comparing any two gaps.

concepts.title: Explaining the Gap: What Decompositions Show
concepts.contentHtml:
To explain a gap, researchers decompose it. They estimate how much of the pay difference can be statistically accounted for by differences in measured characteristics, such as education, experience, hours, occupation and industry, and call the rest unexplained.

The economists Francine Blau and Lawrence Kahn ran this exercise on US survey data from 1980 to 2010. The gap fell considerably over the period. By 2010, conventional human capital variables such as education and experience explained little of it, while differences in occupation and industry remained important.1 The gap also closed more slowly at the top of the pay distribution than in the middle or at the bottom, and women's career interruptions and shorter hours still mattered in high-skilled jobs.

Interpretation begins here, and both sides have strong versions:

  • Choices and trade-offs. Part of the gap may be a compensating differential: lower pay accepted in exchange for features such as shorter or more flexible hours. Blau and Kahn themselves suggest the hours and interruption penalties in high-skilled jobs may partly be of this kind.
  • Constraint and discrimination. The unexplained part may include discrimination. More subtly, the explained part may include it too: if women are steered away from well-paid occupations, or if jobs pay less because women do them, then controlling for occupation hides inequality instead of explaining it away.

Decompositions cannot settle this, because they describe associations, not causes. Unexplained means not accounted for by the variables measured: it could be discrimination, or something unmeasured such as preferences or bargaining. To get at causes you need experiments and natural experiments, the subject of the next concept and of Lesson 6.

concepts.title: Testing for Discrimination: The Motherhood Penalty
concepts.contentHtml:
Decompositions leave discrimination as a residual. Experiments try to catch it directly. In a study published in 2007, the sociologists Shelley Correll, Stephen Benard and In Paik ran two tests.

In a laboratory experiment, student participants rated pairs of equally qualified fictional applicants for a job. The files differed in one detail: one mentioned children, for instance through a memo and membership of a parent-teacher association. Participants said they would hire 84% of the women without children but only 47% of the mothers, and offered the women without children an average of $11,000 more in starting salary.1 Mothers were rated less competent and less committed. Fathers were not penalised; they were rated 5 percentage points more committed than men without children.

Student raters are not real employers, so the team also ran an audit study, sending matched applications to real job advertisements. In the audit study with real employers, childless women received 2.1 times as many callbacks as equally qualified mothers.2

Put the evidence together. A common belief is that the pay gap is mainly about employers paying women less for identical work; the measured gap is mostly about which jobs and hours people end up in. But experiments like this show that discrimination does operate at the point of hiring, and that it falls on mothers in particular. That links the pay gap to children, which is where the strongest recent evidence lies.

title: Children, Time, and Greedy Work
description: Goldin's history, the child penalty, and who does the unpaid work

concepts.title: Claudia Goldin's Long View
concepts.contentHtml:
In October 2023 Claudia Goldin of Harvard was awarded the Nobel memorial prize in economics "for having advanced our understanding of women's labour market outcomes". The labour economics topic introduced her idea of greedy jobs; here is the evidence behind it. Goldin assembled more than 200 years of US data, and her first finding upset a simple story of progress.

Women's participation in paid work did not rise steadily with economic growth. It traced a U-shaped curve: married women's participation fell as the economy moved from farming to industry in the early nineteenth century, then rose with the growth of the service sector in the early twentieth. Part of the old picture was a measurement error. Census takers often recorded a married woman's occupation simply as wife, missing her work on farms, in family businesses and in cottage industries.1

Goldin then showed how expectations and technology shaped careers. Many women who were young in the 1950s made educational choices on the assumption that they would not have long careers, and those choices limited them when they returned to work. From the end of the 1960s, the contraceptive pill gave young women control over the timing of children. Because young women could get the pill in different years in different US states, Goldin and Lawrence Katz could show that it led women to delay marriage and childbirth and to train for careers such as law and medicine.

Finally, Goldin, Marianne Bertrand and Katz found in 2010 that men's and women's earnings start out close, but diverge as soon as the first child arrives. Goldin's explanation is greedy work: many well-paid jobs reward being constantly available, and pay disproportionately more for long, inflexible hours. Where one worker can easily hand over to another, the gap shrinks. Goldin and Katz showed that US pharmacy became a female-majority, highly paid profession with a small gender earnings gap.2

concepts.title: The Child Penalty
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you measure what children do to earnings? Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard used Danish administrative records from 1980 to 2013 and an event study: line up every parent by the year their first child was born, and follow mothers' and fathers' earnings in the years before and after. Before the birth, the two lines run in parallel. Afterwards they split, and they stay apart.

The arrival of children created a gender gap in earnings of around 20% in the long run, coming in roughly equal parts from mothers working less often, working fewer hours and earning lower hourly wages.1 Mothers also moved into more family-friendly firms and were less often promoted to manager. Most striking of all, the share of Danish gender inequality in earnings caused by child penalties rose from about 40% in 1980 to about 80% in 2013: as other causes faded, children became the main one.

The size varies by country. Long-run penalties in women's earnings range from 20 to 25% in Scandinavia to about 30% in the United States and around 60% in Germany. A world atlas covering 134 countries found that where most people farm for subsistence, child penalties are a minuscule part of gender inequality, but as economies develop and work shifts to salaried jobs, they become the dominant cause.

Why do the penalties exist? Two tests narrow the answer. First, in Denmark, adoptive mothers' long-run penalties were virtually identical to biological mothers', which suggests that pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding are not the main driver.2 Second, penalties are transmitted across generations, from parents to daughters but not to sons, consistent with preferences about family and career formed in childhood. Adoptive families differ from others in many ways, so neither test is conclusive alone, but together they point towards norms rather than biology.

concepts.title: The Second Shift, Measured
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1989 the Berkeley sociologist Arlie Hochschild published The Second Shift, based on eight years of interviews with 50 working couples. She found that employed wives still did about 75% of household tasks on average, and that the women in her study put in an average of an extra month a year of unpaid work at home.1 They felt, in her words, always exhausted and always rushing. The phrase second shift entered everyday speech.

Large time-use surveys, in which people record what they do through a day, confirm the unequal split of unpaid work. An ONS analysis published in 2016 found that UK women did an average of 26 hours a week of unpaid work such as cooking, childcare, laundry and cleaning, against 16 hours for men: 60% more. The only area where men did more was transport, including driving and commuting. The American Time Use Survey for 2025 found that on days they did household activities, women spent 2.8 hours on them and men 2.1.

Now the surprise. When the economists Michael Burda, Daniel Hamermesh and Philippe Weil added paid and unpaid work together, using time diaries from 25 countries, they found that in rich northern countries, including the United States, men and women do the same amount of total work on average.2 Women do more unpaid work, men more paid work, and the totals balance. Their surveys also showed that economists, sociologists and the general public mostly believed women did more.

Both findings can be true at once. Totals can balance while the content differs, and the content matters: unpaid work builds no pension, salary history or promotion record. Averages can also hide households where the load on mothers is heavier. Hochschild's extra month was a vivid estimate from a small sample; the large surveys suggest that in rich countries what is unequal is the split of work more than its total.

title: Disputed Frontiers
description: The gender-equality paradox in STEM, the dispute over it, and counting sex and gender

concepts.title: The Gender-Equality Paradox
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a finding that surprises almost everyone. You might expect that the more gender-equal a country, the more women study science and engineering. In 2018 the psychologists Gijsbert Stoet and David Geary reported something else. Using international data on the school achievement of 472,242 adolescents, they found that girls did as well as or better than boys in science in two of every three countries, and that in nearly all countries more girls seemed capable of college-level STEM study than actually enrolled. Yet the sex gap in pursuing STEM degrees grew, rather than shrank, with national gender equality.1 They called it the gender-equality paradox.

Their explanation turned on relative strengths. Even where girls matched boys in science, girls tended to be even stronger in reading, so science was more often a boy's best subject than a girl's. Stoet and Geary also proposed, from a mediation analysis, that life-quality pressures in less gender-equal countries push more girls and women into STEM.

Related evidence fits the broader pattern. Falk and Hermle measured six basic preferences (willingness to take risks, patience, altruism, trust, and positive and negative reciprocity) in 80,000 people across 76 countries, and found that gender differences in preferences were positively related to economic development and gender equality. A 2009 meta-analysis of vocational interest inventories, covering 503,188 respondents, found that men on average prefer working with things and women with people, with a large effect size of 0.93 standard deviations.

The strongest version of this view says that when material constraints loosen, people choose more by interest, and average interests differ by sex. That is a serious hypothesis. The next concept shows why its central evidence has been fiercely contested.

concepts.title: Measurement Under Fire
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2018 and 2019, researchers at Harvard's GenderSci Lab, including the historian of science Sarah Richardson, tried to reproduce the paradox, and found that the numbers did not add up. Poland, for example, had 43.63% women among its STEM graduates, which would rank it fifth of the 45 countries in the study, yet the paper reported a value of 26.9%.1

The explanation was a definitional choice. Stoet and Geary had not reported women's share of STEM graduates. A December 2019 correction of 1,113 words explained that they had used a propensity measure, which can be read as the percentage of women in STEM if equal numbers of men and women enrolled at university.2 Even with that information, Richardson's team could not replicate all the results. When they used Stoet and Geary's own alternative gender-equality index, which adds basic measures of well-being such as health, education and life satisfaction, they reported that there was no paradox to be found.

Stoet and Geary replied that their metric was chosen to capture a woman's likelihood of completing a STEM degree compared with a man's, and that the overall correlation they had found remained the same. The journal's editors judged that a correction, not a retraction, was appropriate.

A second line of attack accepts a pattern but rejects the interpretation. Breda and colleagues measured the stereotype that maths is not for girls among 300,000 fifteen-year-olds in 64 countries. The stereotype was stronger in more egalitarian and developed countries, and could entirely explain the paradox. On this view, development reshapes gender norms rather than removing them; as the sociologist Maria Charles put it, there is no evidence that gender stereotypes are weaker in advanced industrial societies. The dispute therefore has layers: whether the pattern holds under different definitions (measurement), and whether preferences or norms cause it (interpretation).

concepts.title: Counting Sex and Gender Identity
concepts.contentHtml:
Every statistic in this topic rests on a prior decision about what is being counted. For most of their history, official surveys asked about sex and treated it as obvious. That is changing, and the change has proved hard.

Census 2021 in England and Wales asked a new, voluntary question of everyone aged 16 and over: is your gender identity the same as the sex you were registered at birth? About 45.4 million people (93.5%) said yes, 262,000 (0.5%) said no, and 6.0% did not answer.1 Of the no group, 48,000 identified as trans men, 48,000 as trans women and 30,000 as non-binary, while 118,000 gave no further answer. But the ONS later reported patterns suggesting that some respondents, most notably those with lower levels of English language proficiency, may not have interpreted the question as intended. In September 2024 the Office for Statistics Regulation concluded that the estimates did not comply with important quality aspects of the Code of Practice for Statistics, and they became official statistics in development.

The law moved too. On 16 April 2025 the UK Supreme Court ruled that the terms sex, man and woman in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex, not certificated sex.2 The case, For Women Scotland v The Scottish Ministers, turned on statutory wording. The court stressed that it was not deciding the wider public argument about the meaning of gender or sex, and that trans people keep protection against discrimination and harassment.

Each position has a principled core. One holds that sex must be recorded on its own because it predicts outcomes in health, crime, sport and pay, and that merging it with identity degrades the data. The other holds that gender identity is the category that matters most in trans people's lives, and that public systems should recognise it. On data the two need not clash, since a survey can ask both questions. The hard disputes are about which category governs particular spaces, rights and records.
